candidateRows: If the universe is emergent, it emerges from a mind; the universe is emergent, so it emerges from a mind.
This is the formal digital-physics argument whose two premises organize the opening presentations and directly determine the debate's central conclusion.
Michael defines the relevant universe as the experienced macroscopic world or spacetime and presents emergence and mental foundations as the argument's two decisive premises.
Quantum fields are mathematical representations rather than concrete substances, while physical reality appears emergent from underlying information.
The move supplies Michael's main defense of cosmic emergence while attacking the materialist proposal that quantum fields can serve as the final concrete ontology.
James's previously stated view that everything can reduce to physically real quantum fields without positing God.

Michael invokes problems with particle and field interpretations, claims quantum field theory lacks a fundamental substance, and adds holographic considerations as support for informational emergence.
An idealist ontology is more parsimonious because it retains consciousness and informational reality without adding mind-independent material substance.
This is a direct abductive bridge from the alleged informational character of physical reality to idealism and ultimately to a necessary foundational mind.
The materialist contention that a mind-independent physical ontology is simpler and does not require a divine mind.
Michael argues that consciousness is known directly whereas an undetectable material substance is additional ontology, so a purely mental reality and necessary mind are allegedly simpler.
Perfect-being theism provides a simpler necessary foundation with fewer brute facts than any imperfect naturalistic foundational state.
The move defends the comparative parsimony of the proposed divine explanation, a central issue because the opposing ontology is presented as simpler.
Naturalistic proposals that a nonconscious physical state can be the necessary and ontologically simpler foundation of reality.
Michael says God's attributes follow from one core property of absolute perfection, whereas naturalism must accept an imperfect physical foundation and its necessity as brute.
Quantum cognition makes a mental source of emergent spacetime more plausible because cognition and the quantum substrate share mathematical behavior.
This is one of Michael's four expressly identified supports for the first premise that emergent spacetime originates in a mind.
James's earlier characterization of the similarity between quantum cognition models and quantum phenomena as merely coincidental.
Michael argues that successful quantum-formal models of cognition resemble processes associated with emergent spacetime and treats that resemblance as evidence of a shared conceptual nature.
Structural similarities between neural networks and the cosmic web are expected if the universe is the external appearance of a mind.
The claimed neural-cosmic structural correspondence is a distinct evidential strand in Michael's cumulative defense of the argument's first premise.
Michael cites work comparing cortical networks with the cosmic web and applies an idealist account on which brains and the universe can appear externally as representations of minds.
Current quantum-gravity research does not establish with confidence that gravity, space, or time is emergent.
The move directly denies the second premise of the formal argument by challenging the evidential maturity and ontological interpretation of quantum-gravity models.
Michael's premise that the universe, understood as spacetime or the macroscopic world, is known to be emergent.
James distinguishes several possible emergence claims, notes the absence of an established quantum theory of gravity, and emphasizes the many competing speculative models.
Even if spacetime or gravity is emergent, ordinary physical emergence neither makes it unreal nor implies a nonmaterial source.
The move blocks the argument's inference from physical emergence to idealism by offering standard material emergence as an adequate interpretation.
Michael's use of emergent spacetime and informational descriptions to motivate a reality beyond fundamental material structure.
James compares emergent spacetime with temperature and weather, explaining it as higher-level behavior of an underlying quantum structure rather than evidence of illusion or mentality.
Quantum-cognition models do not support a cosmic mind because useful mathematical apparatus need not receive a literal physical interpretation.
The move directly challenges one of Michael's principal bridges from quantum formalism and cognition to the claim that the universe emerges from a mind.
Michael's claim that shared quantum-formal behavior between cognition and fundamental physics supports emergence from a mind.
James treats quantum cognition as a modeling approach for categorization, decisions, and context effects, arguing that predictive success does not establish a physical cognition-quantum connection.
Quantum theorems and experiments constrain viable quantum theories but provide no support for minds playing a role in quantum mechanics.
The move rejects a distinct empirical and theoretical route by which Michael has connected quantum mechanics to mentality and idealist metaphysics.
Michael's prior appeals to Bell inequalities, quantum-eraser experiments, Leggett inequalities, and related results as supporting mental involvement.
James acknowledges that some cited material was more prominent in Michael's earlier presentations, but argues that the results only restrict acceptable quantum theories and do not privilege minds.
Theistic idealism is an ad hoc and unnecessarily complex ontology compared with treating quantum fields or comparable physical entities as fundamental.
This directly advances the motion-level simplicity comparison by arguing that the theistic account adds layered mental, mathematical, and divine entities without explanatory need.
Michael Jones's earlier case that idealist metaphysics best explains emergent physical reality.
After disputing purported quantum support for mind, Fodor maps the layers in Jones's ontology and argues that a fundamental physical ontology is more parsimonious despite interpretive questions.
If humans are simulations or derivatives within God's mind, their sinfulness creates a serious tension with the Christian claim that God is perfectly sinless.
The argument challenges the internal coherence of Jones's specific theistic idealism by connecting its mind-of-God ontology to a central commitment of Christian theology.
Jones's claim that created reality and human minds are derivative from or simulated within God's mind.
Fodor reasons from humanity's derivation within God and humanity's sinfulness to an allegedly sinful part of God, presenting the result as a theological tension for Jones to resolve.
Emergent spacetime undercuts first-cause cosmological arguments because a cosmic beginning can arise from a more fundamental quantum-like state without an immaterial personal cause.
This draws a significant anti-theistic implication from the emergent-spacetime premise that otherwise forms part of Jones's own digital-physics case.
Jones's use of emergent spacetime and digital physics within a broader evidential case for theism.
Fodor accepts for argument that classical spacetime emerges from deeper information or quantum structure, then argues that such emergence supplies a nonpersonal explanation of cosmic beginnings.
Ontic structural realism supports idealism because fundamental physics describes structures and relations without requiring localized material particles or a fundamental material substance.
This supplies a principal scientific and philosophical bridge from quantum field theory to the idealist ontology defended by the pro side.
Fodor's request for the strongest evidence that the universe is emergent and his materialist interpretation of physical theory.
In response to a request for his best evidence, Jones says science refers to relational structure rather than material substance and aligns this view with information-first accounts of reality.
If physical science reduces its fundamental account to mathematical abstractions and information rather than material substances, that result favors an idealist ontology.
The move makes explicit the contested inference from substance-free structural physics to idealism, rather than merely describing structural realism itself.
Fodor's challenge asking what ontological conclusion actually follows from theories describing structural relations.
Jones argues that eliminating classical particles and substances leaves mathematical structure and underlying information, which he presents as the kind of ontology idealists have long proposed.
Structural realism does not entail idealism because abstract mathematical structures describe concrete relata, and relations cannot exist without real things that bear those relations.
This directly blocks the pro side's central inference from structural descriptions in physics to an information-first or idealist metaphysics.
Jones's contention that structural realism and reduction to mathematical abstractions imply an idealistic ontology.
Fodor argues that mathematics is abstract and descriptive, while structural relations presuppose relata; he therefore retains an underlying physical reality governed by physical equations.
A simulated world shows how objects can emerge from code without corresponding internal material particles, supporting an analogy in which physical properties emerge from information grounded in God.
The analogy supplies a concrete model for the pro side's emergence claim and answers the objection that physical relations require fundamental material relata.
Fodor's claim that relations require concrete physical relata and therefore an underlying material substance.
Jones compares physical emergence to a video game whose objects are property bundles generated by code, with the computer analogous to the divine ground, then questions any extra material substrate.

Scientific realism identifies the entities described by successful physical theories with material reality, while adding a divine mental layer beneath that reality makes the ontology more complicated.
This is a sustained defense of the materialist side's core parsimony claim and a direct rebuttal to the allegation that materialism posits an unnecessary extra substance.
Jones's argument that materialism adds an unnecessary substance beyond the structural and informational content described by science.

Fodor says realism requires something beyond predictive theories, identifies that something as material reality, and argues that Jones adds further levels by placing its appearance or simulation in God's mind.
Idealism is simpler because it begins with known conscious agents and one foundational mind, whereas materialism adds an undetectable substrate and further unexplained emergent layers.
This directly reverses Fodor's central parsimony argument and offers the pro side's positive account of why a foundational conscious mind has greater explanatory economy.
Fodor's argument that material reality alone is sufficient and that a simulation or divine mental ground adds needless complexity.

Jones treats consciousness as the known fundamental starting point, reduces material reality to dependent informational properties, and contrasts this with materialism's hidden substrate and emergence problems.
Theistic idealism retains all physical regularities as posits and additionally makes their continued stability depend on God's contingent choices, creating more brute facts than physicalism.
This attacks the claimed explanatory economy of idealism by arguing that it preserves every physical regularity while adding a further unexplained divine-volitional dependence.
Jones's claim that one foundational conscious mind explains reality with fewer posits and brute facts than materialism.
Fodor argues that an idealist must reproduce the entire quantum and spacetime structure in God's mind, yet offers only God's ongoing desire as the explanation for its uniform persistence.
A material substrate constrains possible developments, whereas a divine simulation permits any logically possible development and therefore requires more explanation.
This directly advances the materialist simplicity case by arguing that theism introduces a substantially larger space of unexplained possible outcomes.
Jones's claim that variable natural laws and multiple naturalistic root facts create the same contingency problem for materialism.
The speakers are comparing whether natural laws or divine choices better ground regularity, necessity, and the observed structure of the universe.
A complex divine thought does not entail a complex ontology, and the internal nature of a perfect mental foundation can explain its necessity more economically than brute material properties.
This supplies the principal theistic simplicity response, claiming that one internally intelligible mental foundation is ontologically cheaper than numerous unexplained material facts.
Fodor's argument that divine freedom multiplies brute contingencies and leaves the observed regularities less constrained than materialism does.
Fodor has argued that a material substrate restricts outcomes while God's unconstrained simulation adds explanatory burdens; Jones answers at the ontological level.
Theism shares materialism's unexplained initial contingencies but adds further contingencies because nothing in God's nature fixes the simulated world's details or continuing regularity.
The move develops a central comparative-cost argument: both views face foundational facts, but theistic idealism additionally leaves every later state dependent on discretionary divine choice.
Jones's assertion that a perfect mental foundation explains its own necessity and avoids the many brute facts attributed to material ontology.
The exchange has shifted from whether either view contains brute facts to whether theistic idealism carries additional explanatory liabilities beyond those of material realism.
Inferring an agent from an observed effect need not include an explanation of that agent's motives, just as identifying a killer need not reveal why the crimes occurred.
The analogy supports the broader theistic claim that an explanatory agent can be identified from effects even when the reasons behind particular choices remain unknown.
Fodor's contention that invoking divine choice fails as an explanation unless it accounts for why God selected this world rather than alternatives.
Fodor argues that God's ability to choose any possible world deprives the hypothesis of contrastive explanatory power; Jones disputes the demanded depth of explanation.
A good theory must discriminate among possible observations, but theistic idealism is compatible with virtually every possible outcome and consequently explains too little.
This articulates the governing epistemic standard behind the con case and applies it directly to argue that unrestricted divine simulation lacks predictive and contrastive power.
Jones's analogy that an agent or cause may explain an effect even when the agent's motivations and deeper contingencies are not understood.
After competing analogies about agents and unexplained motives, Fodor formalizes his objection as a general requirement that theories favor some possibilities over others.
An uncaused reality capable of changing states and producing conscious agents effectively grants the theist an agent-like foundation while merely withholding the name God.
The move challenges the distinctiveness of the materialist alternative by arguing that its proposed first cause already possesses the key causal profile sought by theism.
Fodor's earlier position that an atheist can posit a non-divine uncaused foundation for every cosmological role assigned to God.
The discussion moves from explanatory contingency to whether a non-theistic first cause genuinely differs from the kind of foundational agency invoked by cosmological theism.
A non-divine first cause is not God unless it possesses the defining mental and perfect-being attributes, so causal priority alone does not collapse materialism into theism.
This preserves the conceptual separation between a minimal uncaused foundation and the much richer divine ontology, blocking a central identification in the pro argument.
Jones's contention that an uncaused, state-changing source of the universe and conscious agents amounts to God under another description.
Jones has argued that the atheist's cosmological foundation concedes what the theist wants; Fodor responds by specifying the additional attributes required for divinity.
God's compatibility with every logically possible outcome is a weakness rather than a virtue because an unrestricted hypothesis fails to explain why the actual outcome occurred.
This concise formulation connects divine omnipotence to underdetermination and states the core reason the con side regards the God hypothesis as explanatorily weak.
Jones's repeated inference that any foundational cause performing an agent-like creative role is effectively agency or divinity despite lacking mental attributes.
The parties have distinguished a minimal universe-causing state from a conscious perfect being, and the discussion returns to the consequences of God's unrestricted capacities.
The range of possible worlds is vast on both worldviews, so divine freedom does not create a distinctive contingency objection against theistic idealism.
This is the mature pro response to the contrastive-explanation objection, arguing that alternative possibilities burden naturalism and theism in materially equivalent ways.
Fodor's claim that the God hypothesis leaves a uniquely broad range of possible worlds and events unexplained by any constraining foundation.
The debate has narrowed to whether contingency is symmetric at the foundational level or whether divine discretion continues to enlarge possibilities throughout cosmic history.
Even if both views leave initial laws unexplained, material properties constrain all later regularities whereas divine freedom leaves later deviations, miracles, and interventions unconstrained.
This directly answers the pro symmetry defense by locating the comparative advantage of materialism in its continuing constraints rather than in an explanation of initial laws.
Jones's argument that the multiplicity of possible worlds exists equally under naturalism and therefore cannot count specifically against divine freedom.
Jones treats possible-world contingency as shared by both sides; Fodor distinguishes shared uncertainty about initial conditions from the divergent constraints on later events.
Compatibility of cosmological observations with holographic models does not by itself constitute evidence favoring those models.
This distinction directly tests whether the empirical material offered for digital physics actually discriminates in its favor rather than merely permitting it.
Jones's use of the cosmological paper as support for an emergent or holographic universe.
After identifying the displayed paper, Fodor argues that observational compatibility is weak unless the findings positively favor holographic emergence over alternatives.
The cited study was offered to establish observational coherence, while the broader holographic principle is supported as a mainstream route toward quantum gravity.
The move clarifies the intended evidential burden of the study and locates the larger case in black-hole physics and major quantum-gravity programs.
Fodor's objection that observational compatibility alone is not positive evidence for holographic emergence.

Jones says he claimed compatibility rather than exclusive confirmation, then argues that holography remains important because it arose from black-hole physics and informs leading quantum-gravity approaches.
Holographic approaches remain early and unsettled, and their application to black holes must not be conflated with application to the universe as a whole.
This challenges both the claimed maturity of the scientific support and the inference from a recognized local application to a much broader cosmological ontology.
Jones's claim that holography is mainstream physics and the way forward across quantum-gravity research.
Fodor grants that holography is seriously studied but emphasizes the absence of a settled quantum-gravity theory and the difference between black-hole and whole-universe applications.
When leading cosmologists identify holographic emergence as the way forward, it is reasonable to treat it as the presently most probable explanation despite residual uncertainty.
The move supplies the epistemic rule connecting unsettled frontier physics to the debate's abductive conclusion rather than demanding certainty before drawing support.
Fodor's contention that holographic cosmology is too early-stage and uncertain to bear substantial argumentative weight.
Jones answers the uncertainty objection by arguing that possibility of error does not defeat an inference to the explanation most favored by current cosmological research.
If experienced spacetime and material structure emerge from more abstract mathematical relations rather than fundamental matter, that pattern supports an idealist ontology.
This is the principal bridge from emergent spacetime and structural realism to the pro side's metaphysical conclusion that idealism better explains experienced reality.
Fodor's request for an explanation of how emergent gravity or spacetime provides evidence for theistic idealism.
Jones argues that science undermines a fundamental material substrate and instead portrays perceived reality as emerging from mathematical abstractions, which he takes to fit idealism.
Existing emergent-spacetime models derive spacetime or gravity from quantum states, entanglement, or related physical structures, not from a mind.
The move attacks the central inferential bridge from technical emergence results to idealism by showing that the scientific models specify non-mental bases for emergence.
Jones's argument that emergence from abstractions or mathematics supplies scientific support for an idealist ontology.
Fodor outlines entanglement-based, micro-constituent, and holographic models, then argues that their contents concern quantum structures and do not yield Jones's conclusion about mind.
The scientific content that spacetime emerges from entanglement does not provide an argument for a mind, and theistic idealism can be defended independently of those theories.
This precisely isolates the alleged non sequitur at the heart of the digital-physics case: moving from nonfundamental spacetime to a mental foundation.
Jones's claim that his idealist interpretation is a more parsimonious philosophical explanation of the emergence findings.
Fodor grants that physical theories admit philosophical interpretation but insists that their stated mechanisms do not entail mentality and are unnecessary to a purely philosophical idealist case.
Citing physicists for the shared conclusion that spacetime is nonfundamental does not imply endorsing their complete theories or claiming that they endorse idealism.
The clarification defends the legitimacy of using scientific results as premises within a distinct philosophical inference without misattributing the resulting worldview to physicists.
Fodor's objection that the cited emergence theories describe quantum mechanisms rather than emergence from a mind.

Jones says his appeal is limited to the shared data point that spacetime is not fundamental; his idealist conclusion comes from separate philosophical premises and need not be shared by cited scientists.
If every possible scientific finding can be accommodated within theistic idealism, then emergent-spacetime findings do not selectively support the digital-physics argument.
The move challenges the empirical discriminating power and potential falsifiability of the pro case, directly questioning whether its scientific evidence favors the proposed metaphysics.
Jones's claim that scientific findings about emergent spacetime provide evidential support for theistic idealist metaphysics.
Fodor argues that even a discovery of fundamental spacetime could be redescribed as another element in God's mental simulation, making contrary scientific outcomes equally compatible with the view.
Metaphysical views may accommodate many datasets, but evidence still changes their comparative probability because less congenial findings require less parsimonious auxiliary explanations.
This supplies the pro side's answer to the underdetermination objection by explaining how scientific results can confirm or disconfirm a metaphysics without strict logical falsification.
Fodor's argument that theistic idealism is equally consistent with any scientific result and therefore gains no support from emergence.

Jones argues that universal logical compatibility is shared by broad metaphysical systems, while findings such as fundamental spacetime would still count against his view by increasing explanatory costs.
The incarnation is coherent under idealism because physical embodiment is a representation rather than the essence of a person, allowing Christ's essence to enter the simulation.
This reply addresses whether the proposed idealist ontology can coherently accommodate a central Christian commitment rather than merely redescribing embodiment.
The objection that God's full essence cannot enter a simulation occurring within God's own mind.
Fodor presses an analogy with entering one's own dream; Jones responds by rejecting the physicalist identification of personal essence with its embodied representation.
Libertarian divine choices are contingent but unexplained and therefore constitute brute facts, leaving nearly everything beyond God's nature unexplained under theistic idealism.
The move supplies the conceptual distinction underlying Fodor's principal explanatory objection that divine freedom multiplies unexplained facts rather than reducing them.
In response to a question, Fodor distinguishes necessary, contingent, and brute facts, then applies that taxonomy to God's freely chosen actions under idealism.
God's thoughts and decisions can be contingent facts rather than brute facts, since a mind's contingent state does not automatically lack an explanation.
This is Jones's direct answer to the claim that libertarian divine action makes the idealist worldview explanatorily empty or saturated with brute facts.
Fodor's claim that God's free decisions are unexplained brute facts under theistic idealist ontology.
Immediately after Fodor classifies divine choices as brute, Jones denies the inference and distinguishes contingent mental states from fundamentally unexplained facts.
Measurable quantum-field effects do not require a physical substance beneath relational structure, because equivalent effects can emerge from information processing within an idealist ontology.
The move directly defends the debate's idealist ontology against the empirical objection that measurable quantum phenomena establish a mind-independent physical substrate.
The objection that measurable quantum-field effects, such as the Casimir effect, demonstrate an underlying physical substrate.
A question cites the Casimir effect as evidence for physical substrate; Jones argues that observed effects can arise from relations and information without substantial particles.

Scientific success supports realism rather than instrumentalism because the best explanation of reliable theories is that they describe something genuinely existing, including some physical substrate.
This reply gives the materialist-realist counterargument to Jones's structural and informational interpretation of physics and defends ontological commitment to physical reality.
Jones's claim that scientific descriptions of relations and effects function without positing an underlying physical substance.
After Jones treats quantum effects as compatible with informational idealism, Fodor invokes the no-miracles argument and insists successful theories track real physical structure or substrate.

A timeless cause need not be a freely acting agent because alternative causal models, including a timeless quantum substrate producing emergent spacetime, can connect timeless causes to temporal effects.
The argument supplies a naturalistic competitor to divine agency for emergent spacetime and denies that a temporal universe uniquely supports a timeless personal cause.
The claim that only libertarian agent causation can explain how a timeless state produces a temporal effect.
Asked how a timeless state could generate an effect without free agency, Fodor outlines competing theories of causation and uses emergent quantum gravity as a countermodel.
Although a timeless entity may produce spacetime, its apparently agent-like activity is more plausibly explained by treating it as an agent than as an unexplained impersonal brute fact.
This reply converts agreement about a timeless basis of emergent spacetime into an abductive argument for personal agency and therefore for the pro-side ontology.
Fodor's proposal that an impersonal timeless quantum substrate can causally generate emergent space and time.
Jones accepts the possibility of a timeless source of spacetime but argues that its productive, agent-like role is less brute and more probable if personal.
Libertarian freedom undermines explanation because each free choice is an unexplained brute fact, so a reality wholly dependent on God's free choices cannot explain why it has its particular form.
This is a compact restatement of the con side's core objection that adding a freely choosing God does not improve explanatory discrimination over brute contingency.
Jones's affirmation that God possesses libertarian rather than physically caused or compatibilist freedom.
After clarifying Jones's account of divine freedom, Fodor argues that undetermined divine decisions provide no reason for one outcome rather than another.

Personal explanations are not fundamentally distinct from scientific explanations because agent explanations are derived physical explanations, while libertarian choice leaves decisions as brute facts.
The move challenges a major route for claiming that theism is simpler than naturalism by denying an autonomous explanatory category for irreducible personal agency.
Swinburne's proposed distinction between simpler personal explanations and scientific explanations of natural laws.
Asked about Swinburne, Fodor gives a qualified response grounded in reductive naturalism and argues that libertarian agency cannot provide fundamental explanatory improvement.

An explanation must narrow the possible outcomes at least probabilistically; because broad theism rules out very little and can accommodate nearly anything, it has correspondingly little explanatory power.
This move articulates the con side's governing criterion of explanation and applies it directly to the motion's contest between theistic and disciplined materialist accounts.
The challenge that a theory may explain everything without difficulty if it also has evidence, scope, and falsifiability.
Fodor explains that successful theories discriminate among possible observations, contrasts this with narratives compatible with every outcome, and applies the objection to theism.
Materialism should be assessed as one component of a developed worldview and only against the phenomena it is intended to explain.
This supplies Fodor's governing account of explanatory scope and answers the claim that materialism is deficient because it leaves many unrelated questions open.
Jones's contention that materialism and theism should be compared as overall metaphysical worldviews with broad explanatory obligations.
The exchange concerns whether a worldview loses explanatory force by permitting many possibilities; Fodor distinguishes a specific ontological postulate from a complete package of beliefs.
Evidence against fundamental spacetime, idealism, or a necessary informational foundation could substantially reduce the probability of theism.
The answer states concrete empirical conditions under which Jones would revise his position, clarifying that his theistic inference is intended to remain scientifically defeasible.
Asked what could convince him that God probably does not exist, Jones identifies an eternal universe, fundamental spacetime, hidden variables, and underlying material substance as possible defeaters.
A substantially stronger teleological or cosmological case that excludes competing explanations could make God's existence more probable.
The answer specifies Fodor's evidential threshold for theism and explains why existing fine-tuning and related arguments remain insufficient without excluding alternatives.
Fodor is asked what would persuade him that God probably exists; he says generic theism is difficult to test but improved design or cosmological arguments might succeed.
Fodor's case combines scientific underdetermination with the claim that a nondivine material foundation is ontologically simpler than God.
Jones's closing reconstruction condenses the con side's two principal considerations: current science underdetermines ultimate reality and a material basis avoids additional divine agency.
Fodor's earlier argument that limited physical evidence and comparative ontological simplicity favor a nondivine material foundation over God.
During the closing steelman exercise, Jones summarizes Fodor as emphasizing the limits of present science, a simpler material ontology, and resistance to positing divine agency.
Jones infers theistic idealism from emergent spacetime evidence and treats God's necessary mind as the parsimonious ground of derivative reality.
Fodor's reconstruction captures the pro side's complete explanatory chain from physics compatible with emergence to a fundamental divine mind offered as the necessary ground.
Jones's earlier case that emergent spacetime and related physical findings support an idealist ontology ultimately grounded in God's mind.
In the reciprocal steelman, Fodor distinguishes compatibility from physicists' own interpretations and summarizes Jones's claim that all natural reality derives from a necessary mind.
